# One word killed the patent: what the Federal Circuit’s Samsung ruling means for US founders
On 1 October 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit decided *Satius Holding v Samsung Electronics* (case no 25-1446). The court invalidated US patent 6,711,385.
That patent had been granted by the USPTO, survived a formal re-examination and been in litigation since 2018. After all of that, the Federal Circuit struck it down because of a single word: “electric”.
The claim covered an apparatus for “transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air”. Both sides agreed that transmitting electric signals directly over the air is a scientific impossibility.  The claim promised both, and the law held the patent owner to the full promise.
When IAM asked me to analyse the ruling, I summed it up this way: every word in the claim can and will be used against you. Here, one word – which was scientifically impossible to implement – resulted in the downfall of the patent.

If you are a founder who treats patent claims like fine print, this case is written for you.
## What the court actually decided, in plain language
The district court in Delaware invalidated the claims for indefiniteness, meaning the claim’s scope was supposedly unclear. The Federal Circuit reversed that part. The judges, led by Chief Judge Moore, held that the claim was perfectly clear. A skilled engineer reading it would understand exactly what it covered, including the impossible part.

Then the court invalidated the patent anyway, on a different ground: enablement.

# One word killed the patent: what the Federal Circuit’s Samsung ruling means for US founders

USA November 4 2026

On 1 October 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit decided Satius Holding v Samsung Electronics (case no 25-1446). The court invalidated US patent 6,711,385.

That patent had been granted by the USPTO, survived a formal re-examination and been in litigation since 2018. After all of that, the Federal Circuit struck it down because of a single word: “electric”.

The claim covered an apparatus for “transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air”. Both sides agreed that transmitting electric signals directly over the air is a scientific impossibility. Electric signals travel through a physical medium, like a wire. WiFi reaches your laptop as an electromagnetic wave. The claim promised both, and the law held the patent owner to the full promise.

When IAM asked me to analyse the ruling, I summed it up this way: every word in the claim can and will be used against you. Here, one word - which was scientifically impossible to implement - resulted in the downfall of the patent.

If you are a founder who treats patent claims like fine print, this case is written for you.

What the court actually decided, in plain language

The district court in Delaware invalidated the claims for indefiniteness, meaning the claim’s scope was supposedly unclear. The Federal Circuit reversed that part. The judges, led by Chief Judge Moore, held that the claim was perfectly clear. A skilled engineer reading it would understand exactly what it covered, including the impossible part.

Then the court invalidated the patent anyway, on a different ground: enablement.

Here is the distinction that matters for your portfolio:

- Definiteness (section 112(b)) asks, is the scope of the claim clear?
- Enablement (section 112(a)) asks, does the patent teach someone how to make and use the full scope of what is claimed?

# Irfan Lateef Shares Insights with IAM on Key Federal Circuit Enablement Ruling, Satius Holding v. Samsung

October 8, 2026 | Irfan Lateef

Knobbe Martens litigation partner Irfan Lateef was quoted in the IAM article, “U.S. Federal Circuit Raises Stakes for Patent Claim Drafting in Satius Ruling,” discussing the importance of preparing patent claims that can survive enablement challenges during litigation.

The article examines the Federal Circuit’s recent decision in Satius Holding v. Samsung Electronics, in which the court held that Satius’ patent directed to transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air was invalid due to lack of enablement. In its opinion, the court maintained that the patent’s claim language encompassed a scientific impossibility, which could consequently not be enabled by a skilled artisan.

In his comments, Lateef emphasized that patent owners must carefully evaluate their claim language during the patent application process, as even a single word such as “or” can introduce challenges in future litigation. Speaking to Samsung’s success in raising the enablement issue on appeal, he suggested that defendants in patent litigation review asserted claims in detail, including where the language could encompass something scientifically impossible. “Satius provides useful authority for an enablement challenge even when the claim’s meaning is clear,” he added.

keenable.snippet:
In a recent precedential decision that came out on October 1, 2026 (*Satius Holding v. Samsung Electronics)*, the Federal Circuit held that a claim covering a scientifically impossible alternative embodiment may be clear, i.e., definite in its scope, but because an impossible alternative embodiment cannot be made or used, its inclusion may render the claim invalid for lack of enablement. The Federal Circuit therefore rejected the district court’s indefiniteness analysis but affirmed the judgment of invalidity on enablement grounds.

In 2018, Satius Holding (Satius) sued Samsung Electronics (Samsung) in the district court of Delaware, alleging infringement of claims 1, 11, and 18 of U.S. Patent No. [6,711,385](https://patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/16/e2/e7/29deaee05673a9/US6711385.pdf), which concerns a coupler for wireless communications. At issue was language in claim 1 describing “a communications apparatus for *transmitting electric **or** electromagnetic signals over air*” and a coupler that includes “a transformer *communicating the electric **or** electromagnetic signals to the air*.” (Emphasis added.) The use of “or” made the claim broad enough to encompass both electric and electromagnetic signals transmitted over air, setting up the dispute over the scientifically impossible electric-signal alternative.
Samsung argued that the claims were indefinite, i.e., claim scope is not clear, because transmitting electric signals “over air” is scientifically impossible. In Samsung’s view, the phrase “communicating electric signals to the air” merely indicates that electric signals can pass through the communications apparatus. The phrase does not mean electric signals can propagate through the air, as the phrase “over air” would otherwise suggest. *See Satius Holding, Inc. v. Samsung Elecs. Co.*, No. 1:18-cv-850-CJB, D.I. 254, at 6 n.4 (D. Del. Dec. 12, 2024) (*Decision*).

The Federal Circuit held that the claims were not indefinite because their scope was reasonably certain even though they covered a scientifically impossible embodiment. The court nevertheless affirmed invalidity because the claims were not enabled under § 112(a): the full claim scope included an inoperable alternative that a skilled artisan could not make or use. The decision draws a sharp line between unclear claim scope and impossible claim scope: impossibility may defeat enablement even when it does not make the claim indefinite. Affirmed the district court’s final judgment of invalidity, but on lack-of-enablement grounds rather than indefiniteness. Costs awarded to Samsung. The court construed “transmitting electric . . . signals over air” to mean transmitting signals over air in electric form, rejecting Satius’s attempt to read in an electric-to-electromagnetic transformation step. Although that construction covered a scientific impossibility, the claims were definite because the bounds of the claim were clear; there is no per se rule that inoperable embodiments make a claim indefinite. The court distinguished cases where impossible or nonsensical language made it unclear what the inventor regarded as the invention. The Federal Circuit reached enablement despite the district court’s waiver concern because the issue was briefed, reviewed de novo, involved no factual dispute, and remand would serve no purpose. Satius Holding v. Samsung Electronics: Impossible Claims Can Still Be Definite—But Lack Enablement
Overview
On October 1, 2026, the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit clarified the interplay between the indefiniteness and enablement requirements on review of a judgment of invalidity due to an “impossible” claim limitation. In Satius Holding v. Samsung Electronics, the Court concluded that a claim that includes a scientific impossibility may still be definite if it informs with reasonable certainty the scope of the invention. But such a claim would necessarily lack enablement on the grounds that the scientific impossibility cannot be made or used by a skilled artisan.
Background
In 2018, Satius Holding (Satius) sued Samsung Electronics (Samsung), in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware (the District Court), for allegedly infringing claims 1, 11 and 18 of U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385 (the ‘385 Patent). The claims of the ‘385 patent were generally directed to a “communication apparatus for transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air” that includes a coupler with a transformer for “communicating the electric or electromagnetic signals to the air”. See ‘385 Patent, Claim 1 (emphasis added).
During claim construction, Samsung argued that the claims were indefinite on the ground that the transmission of electric signals over air is “scientifically impossible.” The allegedly impossible language had apparently been copied from a previous patent application in which the signals were transmitted over electric lines, which would not be an impossibility.

Federal Circuit Affirms Invalidity Challenge to Scientifically Impossible Claim Language on Enablement Grounds

October 23, 2026
Authored and Edited by Erin M. Lynch ; Christopher B. Anderson ; Erik R. Puknys
In Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd., No. 25-1446 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026) , the Federal Circuit affirmed an invalidity finding for Satius’ U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385 but did so on enablement grounds rather than the indefiniteness grounds relied on by the district court.
Satius sued Samsung for infringement of the ’385 patent, which claims a communications apparatus capable of transmitting electric (along with electromagnetic) signals over air—a feat that both parties agreed is scientifically impossible. As a result, the district court held the asserted claims indefinite and entered a final judgment of invalidity in favor of Samsung. Satius appealed, challenging the finding of indefiniteness. In reply, Samsung argued that the claims were invalid for lack of enablement even if found to be definite.
On appeal, the Federal Circuit rejected the district court's indefiniteness ruling, holding that, despite the scientific impossibility of transmitting electric signals over air, the claims still allow a skilled artisan to understand the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty, thus satisfying the definiteness requirement. The Court nevertheless affirmed invalidity on enablement grounds, exercising its discretion to reach the issue because it had been fully briefed on appeal. Emphasizing that § 112(a) requires the specification to enable the full scope of the claims, the Court held that claims encompassing a scientifically impossible embodiment are inoperable and therefore not enabled.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
Docket Number: 25-1446
Date Decided: October 1, 2026
Justia Opinion Summary
Satius Holding, LLC brought a lawsuit against Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. and Samsung Electronics America, Inc., alleging infringement of claims 1, 11, and 18 of its U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385. The patent concerns a communications apparatus with a coupler designed to match impedances between air and a wireless transmitter/receiver. A central issue was whether the patent's claims, which include transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air, are valid given that transmitting electric signals over air is scientifically impossible.
The United States District Court for the District of Delaware initially stayed the case pending reexamination by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, which rejected independent claim 1 but upheld dependent claims 11 and 18. After the stay was lifted, the District Court conducted claim construction and found claims 1, 11, and 18 to be indefinite, entering a final judgment of invalidity for those claims. Satius appealed this judgment to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.
The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit reviewed the District Court’s findings de novo. It determined that, although transmitting electric signals over air is impossible, the claims were not indefinite because their scope was clear to skilled artisans. However, the court concluded that the claims failed the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), as the patent specification did not enable the full scope of the invention, including the scientifically impossible embodiments. By Madhumita “Mita” Datta, PhD, Kaelyn Shinbashi

I. **Summary:**

In a recent precedential decision that came out on October 1, 2026 (*Satius Holding v. Samsung Electronics)*, the Federal Circuit held that a claim covering a scientifically impossible alternative embodiment may be clear, i.e., definite in its scope, but because an impossible alternative embodiment cannot be made or used, its inclusion may render the claim invalid for lack of enablement. In Samsung’s view, the phrase “communicating electric signals to the air” merely indicates that electric signals can pass through the communications apparatus. The phrase does not mean electric signals can propagate through the air, as the phrase “over air” would otherwise suggest. *See Satius Holding, Inc. v. Samsung Elecs. Co.*, No. 1:18-cv-850-CJB, D.I. 254, at 6 n.4 (D. Del. Dec. 12, 2024) (*Decision*).

In 2018, Satius Holding (Satius) sued Samsung Electronics (Samsung), in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware (the District Court), for allegedly infringing claims 1, 11 and 18 of U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385 (the ‘385 Patent).
